title: A hundred years asleep
hook: a man passes a ruined town, dies a hundred years, and wakes to see his donkey raised (2:259)
carry: he can revive what is dead

segments.voice: Yesterday: no compulsion, and your line was a handhold you grasp yourself. Did you let someone hold their view in peace? Today, a man who asks a hard question out loud, and is answered with a story he lives through. Day three hundred fifty-eight.

A traveler rides his donkey past a town that's been destroyed. Roofs fallen in, walls collapsed onto themselves, nobody left. He's carrying some food and something to drink. He stops, looks at the ruins, and says what anyone might say: how could God ever bring this back to life? The text doesn't say whether he asks it in wonder or in doubt. It's the question that comes standing in front of something truly finished. And then, the Qur'an says, he finds out. Today: a hundred years asleep.
screen: `A RUINED TOWN, NOBODY LEFT.` → `HOW COULD THIS EVER LIVE AGAIN?` → `THEN HE FINDS OUT.`

segments.voice: Verse two hundred fifty-nine goes on: God caused him to die for a hundred years, then raised him. And asked him: how long have you stayed? He answered: a day, or part of a day. That's how it feels to wake. No, a hundred years. Now look at your food and drink: they haven't spoiled. And look at your donkey. And look at the bones, how We set them together and then clothe them with flesh. And when it became clear to him, he said: I know that God has power over all things. The Qur'an doesn't name the man or the town. The commentators offer names: some say 'Uzayr, whom some identify with Ezra, and the town Jerusalem after its destruction; others name the prophet Jeremiah, or someone else. The text stays silent, and the story works without a name. Look at the details it does give. The food is unchanged after a century. The donkey, in one reading, has gone to bones and comes back; other commentators read the bones as the man's own. One thing time didn't touch, one thing it took completely, and in the story both are in God's hands. Now look where the story sits. Just before it, Ibrahim tells a king: my Lord gives life and causes death. Just after it, Ibrahim asks to see how the dead are raised, and is shown with four birds. Three stories in a row about the same question. The man's question isn't scolded. It's answered with a demonstration he lives through. He can revive what is dead.
screen: `A DAY, OR PART OF A DAY` · `THE FOOD UNSPOILED, THE DONKEY RAISED` · `THE TEXT DOESN'T NAME HIM` · `THREE STORIES, ONE QUESTION`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at something old coming back to life. A tree putting out new leaves after winter. A friendship you thought was over that's started again. An old skill coming back to your hands. Bring one to mind and look at it closely: what was dead about it, and what's stirring now? If you pray, you can hold it up with the man's last words: I know that God has power over all things. The bell holds the time.
'Uzayr. The name some commentators give the man who doubted a ruined town could live, was made to die a century, and woke to see his donkey raised. Today's word.
Your line: he can revive what is dead. Today, give one thing you'd written off, a plant, a hope, a friendship, one more look. Day three hundred fifty-eight.

howItsDone: Muslims read 2:258–260 together as three stories about God giving life to the dead, and often recall them when speaking of resurrection and of hope after loss.

fork.setup: you stand before a ruined town and ask: how could God ever bring this back to life? what happens to you in the story?
options: you're shown: made to die a century, then raised.
fork.reveal: the question is answered, vividly: a hundred years, food unspoiled, a donkey raised from bones. he ends: I know God has power over all things.

original.note: Arabic: a hundred years, the span the man was made to die in 2:259.

trapdoor: what you thought: a strange tale of a long sleep.
what it means: a doubter answered by living through the answer: a ruin, a century, and life restored.
what a scholar hears: an unnamed figure whom commentators identify variously as 'Uzayr or Jeremiah, placed between Ibrahim's two stories in 2:258 and 2:260.

sources.ref: Qur'an 2:258 and 2:260 (Ibrahim and the king; Ibrahim and the four birds)
Tafsir at-Tabari and Ibn Kathir on 2:259 (identity of the man and the town)

notes: Identifications ('Uzayr, Jeremiah, others; Jerusalem after its destruction) are from the commentaries; 'Uzayr's identification with Ezra is common but debated. Confirm wording.
The man is described as asking sincerely ('it isn't a sneer'); commentators differ on whether he was a believer or a doubter. Confirm.
The 'one thing time didn't touch, one thing it took' reading is the writer's observation, not attributed to a commentator.

Editor review (2026-10-01): the narrator no longer rules on the man's motive ('it isn't a sneer' became 'the text doesn't say whether in wonder or doubt'); 'many say 'Uzayr' became 'some say'; the text doesn't say whose bones are clothed with flesh (commentators differ: the donkey's or the man's), so the teach now says so; cut the superlative 'the most vivid demonstration in the surah'.
